items.question: Two identical steel balls, P and Q, leave the edge of a horizontal table at the same instant. P is released from rest and falls vertically. Q is projected horizontally from the edge at 3.0 m s^-1. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement is correct? A: P lands first, because Q has further to travel; B: Q lands first, because it has the greater initial speed; C: P and Q land at the same time, and Q lands with the greater speed; D: P and Q land at the same time, and with the same speed.
items.answer: C: P and Q land at the same time, and Q lands with the greater speed
steps: The vertical and horizontal motions of a projectile are independent.
Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g, so they fall the same height in the same time. A and B are wrong.
The vertical speed on landing is the same for both balls, but Q also keeps its horizontal speed of 3.0 m s^-1.
Speed on landing = sqrt(vx² + vy²), so Q lands with the greater speed. D is wrong, so the answer is C.

items.question: The displacement-time graph for a trolley moving along a straight track is a curve. Its gradient is positive at first, decreases steadily and becomes zero at t = 4.0 s. Which statement describes the motion of the trolley? A: it moves with constant velocity, then stops suddenly at 4.0 s; B: it speeds up steadily until 4.0 s; C: it returns to its starting point at 4.0 s; D: it slows down steadily and is momentarily at rest at 4.0 s.
items.answer: D: it slows down steadily and is momentarily at rest at 4.0 s
steps: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is the velocity.
A positive gradient that decreases steadily means the velocity is positive and falling steadily, so the trolley decelerates.
A zero gradient at 4.0 s means the velocity is zero at that instant, so the trolley is momentarily at rest.
A would give a straight line then a flat line; B needs an increasing gradient; C needs the displacement to fall back to zero, which needs a negative gradient. The answer is D.

steps: The resultant is largest when the forces act in the same direction: 5.0 + 12 = 17 N.

items.question: A book rests on a horizontal table. Which pair of forces is a Newton's third law pair? A: the weight of the book and the upward force of the table on the book; B: the weight of the book and the downward force of the book on the table; C: the upward force of the table on the book and the weight of the table; D: the upward force of the table on the book and the downward force of the book on the table.
items.answer: D: the upward force of the table on the book and the downward force of the book on the table
steps: A Newton's third law pair consists of two forces of the same type, equal in size and opposite in direction, that act on two different bodies and arise from the same interaction.
The table pushes up on the book (a contact force) and the book pushes down on the table (a contact force): same type, equal and opposite, on different bodies. This is D.
A is wrong: both forces act on the book and they balance each other, which is the first law, not the third. They are also different types of force.
B is wrong because the weight is a gravitational force, so its third-law partner is the book's pull on the Earth. C involves the table's weight, which is not part of the same interaction.

items.question: A crane lifts a container of mass 850 kg using a vertical cable. At one instant the tension in the cable is 9.6 kN. Calculate the acceleration of the container at this instant.
steps: Weight of container = m g = 850 x 9.81 = 8338.5 N.

a = resultant force / mass = 1261.5 / 850 = 1.48 m s⁻² = 1.5 m s⁻² upwards.

items.question: State Newton's third law of motion and explain why the two forces in a third-law pair do not cancel each other out.
items.answer: If A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A; the forces act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel.
steps: When body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts a force on A (the two forces form an interaction pair)
The two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
The forces act on different bodies, and forces cancel only if they act on the same body, so they cannot cancel
accept: The two forces are of the same type (for example both gravitational or both contact forces)
The two forces exist at the same time and one cannot exist without the other
Example: the Earth pulls on a book and the book pulls on the Earth with equal and opposite forces
A resultant is found only by adding forces that act on one body

items.question: A box of mass m is at rest on a rough slope that is inclined at an angle theta to the horizontal. What is the frictional force acting on the box? A: mg cos(theta); B: mg sin(theta); C: mg tan(theta); D: mg.
steps: The box is in equilibrium, so the resultant force on it is zero.
Along the slope, the component of the weight down the slope is mg sin(theta). The only other force along the slope is friction, acting up the slope.
So the frictional force = mg sin(theta), which is B.
mg cos(theta) is the component of the weight perpendicular to the slope, which is balanced by the normal reaction force. C and D do not correspond to any component of the weight along the slope.

items.question: Explain why the braking distance of a car is longer on a wet road than on a dry road when the car brakes from the same initial speed.
items.answer: Less friction on a wet road gives a smaller maximum braking force and deceleration, so the braking distance s = u² / (2a) is longer.
steps: The braking force on the car is the frictional force between the tyres and the road
Water reduces the maximum friction, so the braking force is smaller and the deceleration (a = F / m) is smaller
For the same initial speed s = u² / (2a), so a smaller deceleration gives a longer braking distance
accept: The tyres may skid or aquaplane on a layer of water, reducing friction further
The same kinetic energy must be removed by work done against friction (W = F s), so a smaller force needs a longer distance
The thinking distance is unchanged, but the total stopping distance is longer

items.question: Two trolleys collide on a horizontal track and friction is negligible. The collision is inelastic. Which statement about the total momentum and the total kinetic energy of the trolleys is correct? A: the total momentum decreases and the total kinetic energy decreases; B: the total momentum is conserved and the total kinetic energy is conserved; C: the total momentum decreases and the total kinetic energy is conserved; D: the total momentum is conserved and the total kinetic energy decreases.
items.answer: D: the total momentum is conserved and the total kinetic energy decreases
steps: Momentum is conserved in every collision when no external resultant force acts. Friction is negligible, so the total momentum is conserved.
In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms (thermal energy, sound, deformation), so the total kinetic energy decreases.
This is D. A and C wrongly say momentum decreases; B describes an elastic collision.

items.question: A trolley of mass 0.40 kg moving at 1.5 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary trolley of mass 0.60 kg. The trolleys stick together and move off with a common velocity. What is the speed of the trolleys after the collision? A: 0.60 m s⁻¹; B: 0.75 m s⁻¹; C: 1.0 m s⁻¹; D: 1.5 m s^-1.

items.question: State the two conditions that must be satisfied for a rigid body acted on by coplanar forces to be in equilibrium.
items.answer: The resultant force on the body is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero.
steps: The resultant (vector sum of the) force on the body is zero
The sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point (the resultant moment is zero)

items.answer: Force at A = 150 N; force at C = 300 N (both upwards)
steps: The weight of the beam acts at its centre, 3.0 m from A. C is 6.0 - 1.5 = 4.5 m from A, so the weight is 1.5 m from C.

items.question: A tall bus with a high centre of gravity is parked on a road that slopes sideways. Explain why the bus is more likely to topple over than a low sports car on the same road.
items.answer: The vehicle topples once the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside the wheels; a high centre of gravity reaches this at a smaller tilt.
steps: The weight acts vertically downwards through the centre of gravity
If the vertical line through the centre of gravity falls outside the base (the downhill wheels), the weight has a resultant moment about those wheels that turns the vehicle over
A higher centre of gravity moves this line outside the base at a smaller angle of tilt, so the bus topples more easily
accept: A low centre of gravity means the vehicle must tilt much further before the line of the weight passes outside the base
A wider wheelbase (larger base) makes a vehicle more stable
Passengers on an upper deck or luggage on the roof raise the centre of gravity and make toppling more likely
Inside the base the weight gives a restoring moment about the downhill wheels

items.question: A ball is released from rest at a height of 1.50 m above a hard floor and rebounds to a height of 1.10 m. Describe the energy transfers from the moment of release to the top of the first rebound, and explain why the ball does not return to its original height.
items.answer: Gravitational potential energy goes to kinetic energy, then to elastic energy and back to kinetic energy at the impact, but some energy is dissipated as thermal energy and sound, so the ball rises to a lower height.

At the impact the kinetic energy is transferred to elastic potential energy of the compressed ball, and then back to kinetic energy as it rebounds
Some energy is dissipated as thermal energy and sound at the impact, so the ball has less kinetic energy after the bounce and rises to a lower height (less gravitational potential energy at the top)
accept: While rising, kinetic energy is transferred back to gravitational potential energy
Total energy is conserved, but some is transferred to the surroundings and is no longer useful
Air resistance transfers a little energy to thermal energy in the air during the flight
Rebound height 1.10 m / 1.50 m shows that about 27% of the ball's energy has been dissipated

items.question: A metal wire of length L and diameter d extends by x when a tensile force F is applied. A second wire of the same metal has length 2L and diameter d/2. What is the extension of the second wire when a force 2F is applied? Assume that both wires obey Hooke's law. A 4x, B 8x, C 16x, D 32x
steps: Extension = F L / (A E), so for the same material the extension is proportional to F L / d^2.
F doubles (x2), L doubles (x2) and d² becomes (d/2)² = d² / 4 (x4), so the extension is 2 x 2 x 4 = 16 times larger.
A ignores the change in area, B has d instead of d², D has d^3.

items.question: A metal wire is stretched by gradually increasing the tensile force. Explain the difference between the limit of proportionality and the elastic limit of the wire.
items.answer: Beyond the limit of proportionality extension is no longer proportional to force (Hooke's law fails). Beyond the elastic limit the wire does not return to its original length when the force is removed (plastic deformation).
steps: Limit of proportionality: the point beyond which force (or stress) is no longer directly proportional to extension (or strain).
Elastic limit: the point beyond which the wire is permanently deformed and does not return to its original length when the force is removed.
accept: Up to the limit of proportionality the wire obeys Hooke's law.
Beyond the elastic limit the deformation is plastic.
The elastic limit is at or just beyond the limit of proportionality for most metals.

items.question: A copper wire of length 2.40 m and diameter 0.50 mm extends by 1.8 mm when a tensile force of 18 N is applied. The wire obeys Hooke's law. Calculate the Young modulus of copper.
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi (0.25 × 10⁻³)² = 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m², so stress = F / A = 18 / 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ = 9.17 × 10⁷ Pa.
Strain = extension / original length = 1.8 × 10⁻³ / 2.40 = 7.50 x 10^-4.
E = stress / strain = 9.17 × 10⁷ / 7.50 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.2 × 10¹¹ Pa.

items.question: A student finds the Young modulus of a copper wire from the gradient of a graph of force against extension. The wire has unstretched length 2.50 m +/- 0.010 m and diameter 0.300 mm +/- 0.005 mm, and the uncertainty in the gradient is 2.0%. Evaluate which measurement contributes most to the uncertainty in the Young modulus, and calculate the percentage uncertainty in the Young modulus.
items.answer: The diameter contributes most (3.3% since d is squared). Total percentage uncertainty in E = 5.7%.
steps: Percentage uncertainties: diameter 0.005 / 0.300 x 100 = 1.7%; length 0.010 / 2.50 x 100 = 0.4%; gradient 2.0%.
E is proportional to gradient x L / d², so the diameter's percentage uncertainty is doubled: 2 x 1.7 = 3.3%.
Total percentage uncertainty = 2.0 + 0.4 + 3.3 = 5.7%.
The diameter contributes most, so measuring it more precisely would improve the result most.

Take more diameter readings along the wire and average them to reduce its uncertainty.
The length contributes least because it is measured to a small fraction of its value.

A correct example of each, such as light or water waves (transverse) and sound (longitudinal).

items.question: In an experiment to measure the speed of sound, a microphone is moved away from a loudspeaker, driven at 2.50 kHz, through 10 wavelengths. The distance moved is 1.36 m, measured with a metre rule to within +/- 0.005 m. Explain why moving the microphone through 10 wavelengths gives a more precise value for the wavelength than moving it through one wavelength. Support your answer with calculations of the percentage uncertainty.
items.answer: The same absolute uncertainty is a much smaller fraction of a longer distance: about 0.4% for 1.36 m (10 wavelengths) compared with about 3.7% for one wavelength (0.136 m).
steps: Percentage uncertainty in one wavelength = 0.005 / 0.136 x 100 = 3.7%.
Percentage uncertainty in 10 wavelengths = 0.005 / 1.36 x 100 = 0.37%.
The same absolute uncertainty is a smaller percentage of the larger distance, so dividing by 10 gives a more precise wavelength (and speed).
accept: The uncertainty in the wavelength is 0.005 / 10 = 0.0005 m when 10 wavelengths are measured.
A larger number of wavelengths reduces the percentage uncertainty in the speed of sound.
Averaging over many wavelengths reduces the effect of the reading error at the start and end positions.

items.question: State the conditions necessary for two sources of light to be coherent. Explain why two separate filament lamps do not produce an observable interference pattern.
items.answer: Coherent sources have the same frequency (wavelength) and a constant phase difference. Two filament lamps emit light in short random wave trains, so the phase difference between them changes rapidly and randomly and no stable pattern forms.
steps: Coherent sources have the same frequency (or wavelength).
Coherent sources have a constant (fixed) phase difference.
Separate filament lamps emit light as short random wave trains, so the phase difference between them changes randomly and rapidly and no stable pattern forms.
accept: Light is emitted by many atoms independently, so there is no fixed phase relationship between the lamps.
Any fringes would shift too rapidly to be seen, so the intensity appears uniform.
Coherent light can be obtained by splitting one source into two (for example with a double slit) or by using a laser.

A microphone at point P is 3.40 m from A and 4.00 m from B. Deduce whether the microphone detects a maximum or a minimum of loudness at P.
items.answer: Minimum: the path difference of 0.60 m is 1.5 wavelengths, so the sound waves arrive in antiphase.
steps: Wavelength lambda = v / f = 340 / 850 = 0.40 m.
Path difference = 4.00 - 3.40 = 0.60 m = 1.5 lambda.
A path difference of an odd number of half wavelengths (3 lambda / 2) means the waves arrive in antiphase (phase difference 3 pi rad), so they interfere destructively: a minimum.

items.question: A pipe of length 0.45 m is closed at one end and open at the other. A loudspeaker near the open end produces sound of gradually increasing frequency. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s^-1. Ignore end corrections. Calculate the two lowest frequencies at which the air column in the pipe resonates.
items.answer: Lowest frequency = 189 Hz; next frequency = 567 Hz
steps: There is a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.
Lowest frequency: L = lambda / 4, so lambda = 4 x 0.45 = 1.80 m and f = v / lambda = 340 / 1.80 = 189 Hz.
Next resonance: L = 3 lambda / 4, so lambda = 0.600 m.
f = 340 / 0.600 = 567 Hz (three times the lowest frequency).

items.question: A string of length 0.800 m is stretched between two fixed points. The tension in the string is 36 N and its mass per unit length is 6.25 × 10⁻⁴ kg m^-1. The string is plucked at its centre. Explain how a stationary wave is formed on the string.
items.answer: The wave travelling along the string reflects at the fixed ends. The incident and reflected waves (same frequency and amplitude) travelling in opposite directions superpose to give nodes and antinodes.
steps: The wave travelling along the string is reflected at the fixed ends.
The incident and reflected waves (same frequency and wavelength, travelling in opposite directions) superpose.

At nodes the waves are always in antiphase (destructive interference, no movement); at antinodes they are in phase (constructive interference, maximum amplitude), giving a pattern that does not travel along the string.
accept: There is a node at each fixed end.
Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart.
A stationary wave does not transfer energy along the string.

New speed v = sqrt(64 / 6.25 × 10⁻⁴) = 320 m s^-1.

items.question: A ray of light in air is incident on a glass block of refractive index 1.52 at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees. What is the angle of refraction in the glass? A 26 degrees, B 78 degrees, C 25 degrees, D 65 degrees
steps: Snell's law: sin i = n sin r, so sin r = sin 40 / 1.52 = 0.423.
r = 25.0 degrees, so about 25 degrees.
A divides the angle itself by n; B uses sin r = n sin i; D is 90 - 25, the angle between the ray and the surface.

B is sin C, C is tan C and D is 1 / cos C.

items.question: Unpolarised light from a lamp passes through a polarising filter and then through a second polarising filter. As the second filter is rotated, the intensity of the transmitted light changes from a maximum to zero and back to a maximum. Explain what these observations show about the nature of light.
items.answer: Light is a transverse wave. The first filter passes only oscillations in one plane; the second passes none of this light when its transmission direction is at 90 degrees to the first, so the light must be plane polarised, which only transverse waves can be.
steps: The first filter transmits only the oscillations in one plane, so the light that emerges is plane polarised.
The second filter transmits no light when its transmission direction is at 90 degrees to that of the first (and a maximum when they are parallel).
Only transverse waves can be polarised, so light is a transverse wave.
accept: Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.
The intensity goes from maximum to zero twice in one full rotation of the second filter.
The oscillations of light are at right angles to its direction of travel.

items.question: State two conditions that must be met for total internal reflection to occur at a boundary between two transparent media. Calculate the critical angle for light travelling from glass of refractive index 1.62 into air.
items.answer: Conditions: light travels from a medium of higher refractive index to one of lower refractive index, and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle. Critical angle = 38.1 degrees
steps: Condition 1: the light travels from the optically denser medium (higher refractive index) towards the less dense medium.
Condition 2: the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.
At the critical angle the angle of refraction is 90 degrees, so n sin C = 1 and sin C = 1 / 1.62 = 0.617.
C = 38.1 degrees.
accept: The critical angle is the angle of incidence that gives an angle of refraction of 90 degrees.
The light travels from glass to air (a medium of smaller refractive index).
C = 38 degrees to two significant figures.

items.question: Monochromatic light passes through a single narrow slit and forms a pattern on a distant screen. State how the width of the central bright fringe changes when the slit is made narrower, and explain why.
items.answer: The central bright fringe becomes wider, because the narrower the gap the more the waves diffract (spread out) as the gap width gets closer to the wavelength.
steps: The central bright fringe becomes wider.
Diffraction (spreading of the waves) is greater when the width of the gap is closer to the wavelength of the light.
A narrower slit spreads the light through a larger angle, so the central maximum is wider.
accept: The central maximum also becomes less bright because less light passes through the slit.
The angle of the first minimum is given by sin theta = lambda / slit width, so a smaller width gives a larger angle.
The width of the central maximum is inversely proportional to the slit width.

items.question: Light from a laser is directed at right angles to a diffraction grating that has 300 lines per mm. A screen is placed 2.00 m from the grating. The first-order maxima are 0.398 m either side of the central maximum. Show that the angle between the central maximum and a first-order maximum is about 11 degrees.

theta = 11.3 degrees, which is about 11 degrees.

items.question: Light from a laser is directed at right angles to a diffraction grating that has 300 lines per mm. A screen is placed 2.00 m from the grating, and the first-order maxima are 0.398 m either side of the central maximum. Calculate the wavelength of the light from the laser.

n lambda = d sin theta with n = 1, so lambda = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ x sin(11.25 degrees) = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ x 0.1952.
lambda = 6.51 × 10⁻⁷ m, i.e. 651 nm.

items.answer: Highest order = 5 (sin theta cannot exceed 1, so n <= d / lambda = 5.12)
steps: The maximum possible value of sin theta is 1, so n lambda <= d.
n must be a whole number, so the highest order is 5.

items.question: An electron and a proton are each accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. What is the approximate value of (de Broglie wavelength of the electron) / (de Broglie wavelength of the proton)? A 0.023, B 43, C 1.0, D 1800
steps: Both gain the same kinetic energy E_k = e V. Since p = sqrt(2 m E_k), p is proportional to sqrt(m).
lambda = h / p, so lambda_e / lambda_p = sqrt(m_p / m_e) = sqrt(1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹) = 43.
A is the inverse; C would need equal momenta; D is m_p / m_e, which comes from assuming equal speeds.

items.question: Light of frequency below the threshold frequency of a zinc plate does not cause photoelectric emission, however intense the light is. Explain this observation using the photon model of light.
items.answer: Each electron absorbs a single photon of energy hf. If hf is less than the work function no electron gains enough energy to escape, and a greater intensity only gives more photons per second, not more energy per photon.
steps: Light consists of photons, each with energy E = h f, and one electron interacts with one photon.
Below the threshold frequency the photon energy is less than the work function (h f < phi), so an electron cannot escape from the surface.
Increasing the intensity only increases the number of photons per second, not the energy of each photon, and electrons cannot build up energy from several photons, so there is still no emission.
accept: Wave theory predicts that energy would build up over time and release electrons, which is not observed.
No emission occurs even after a long exposure time.
The work function is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface.

items.answer: (i) Maximum kinetic energy = 9.0 × 10⁻²⁰ J; (ii) stopping potential = 0.56 V
steps: Photon energy E = h c / lambda = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ x 3.00 × 10⁸ / (450 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Work function = 2.20 x 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.52 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

items.question: Electrons accelerated through a potential difference pass through a thin sheet of graphite and produce a pattern of rings on a fluorescent screen. The accelerating potential difference is increased. Explain what happens to the radius of the rings on the screen, and why the pattern provides evidence for the wave nature of electrons.

items.question: The technetium-99m sample has an initial activity of 400 MBq and the half-life of technetium-99m is 6.0 hours. Calculate the number of technetium-99m nuclei in the sample when its activity is 400 MBq.
items.answer: N = 1.2 × 10¹³ nuclei (1.25 × 10¹³ to 3 s.f.; decay constant 3.21 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹).
steps: Half-life T = 6.0 x 3600 = 2.16 × 10⁴ s.
Decay constant lambda = ln 2 / T = 3.21 × 10⁻⁵ s^-1.
Activity A = lambda N, so N = A / lambda = 4.00 × 10⁸ / 3.21 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.25 × 10¹³ nuclei.

items.question: Technetium-99m emits gamma radiation only and has a half-life of 6.0 hours. Evaluate its suitability as a tracer injected into the body, compared with an alpha-emitting isotope of half-life 100 years.
items.answer: Suitable: gamma leaves the body and is weakly ionising, and the short half-life keeps the dose low; a 100-year alpha emitter is not.
steps: Gamma radiation is penetrating, so it leaves the body and can be detected outside, whereas alpha radiation would be absorbed in the tissue
Gamma radiation is weakly ionising, so it causes much less damage to cells than alpha particles absorbed inside the body
A half-life of 6 hours is long enough to complete the scan, but the activity falls to a very small value within a day or two, so the total dose is small
An isotope with a half-life of 100 years would remain active in the body for the rest of the patient's life, giving a continuing dose

A short half-life gives a high activity from a small number of nuclei, so a small amount of tracer gives a detectable signal
A source with a half-life of 100 years has a very low activity from a given number of nuclei, so would need a large amount of material

items.answer: D: charge +1 e and baryon number 0
steps: The anti-strange quark has charge +1/3 e, so the charge of the meson is +2/3 + 1/3 = +1 e.
Each quark has baryon number +1/3 and each antiquark -1/3, so the baryon number is +1/3 - 1/3 = 0, as for all mesons. This is option D.

items.question: Protons are accelerated from rest at the centre of a cyclotron until they leave at the maximum radius of the dees. The magnetic flux density is unchanged but the alternating potential difference across the gap between the dees is doubled. Which row describes the kinetic energy of the protons when they leave and the number of revolutions they make? A kinetic energy doubles and number of revolutions halves, B kinetic energy doubles and number of revolutions unchanged, C kinetic energy unchanged and number of revolutions halves, D kinetic energy unchanged and number of revolutions doubles
items.answer: C: kinetic energy unchanged and number of revolutions halves
steps: At the maximum radius R the speed is fixed by B q v = m v² / R, so v = B q R / m and the final kinetic energy q² B² R² / (2m) does not depend on the p.d.
In each revolution the protons cross the gap twice and gain 2qV, so the number of revolutions = final kinetic energy / (2qV).
Doubling V halves the number of revolutions: option C. A and B wrongly make the final energy depend on V; D inverts the effect on the number of revolutions.

items.question: In Rutherford's experiment, most alpha particles passed through a thin gold foil with little or no deflection, but about 1 in 8000 was deflected through more than 90 degrees. Explain what these two observations show about the structure of the atom.
items.answer: Most of the atom is empty space, and the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a very small, dense nucleus.
steps: Most alpha particles pass straight through, so most of the atom is empty space
A few are deflected through large angles, so they meet a strong repulsive force from a concentrated region of positive charge (the nucleus)

Only about 1 in 8000 is deflected through a large angle, so the nucleus is very small compared with the atom, and it contains most of the mass because it can reverse the motion of the massive alpha particle

items.question: A free electron of kinetic energy 12.5 eV collides with a hydrogen atom in its ground state. The first four energy levels are -13.6 eV, -3.40 eV, -1.51 eV and -0.85 eV. Deduce to which of these levels the atom could be excited by the collision.

steps: In a very massive star gravity compresses the core to a much higher temperature, so successive fusion stages build heavier elements, up to iron

In a Sun-like star the core never becomes hot enough for the later stages of fusion; it expels its outer layers as a planetary nebula and the core remains as a white dwarf

items.question: The diameter d of a wire is measured as 0.52 mm with an absolute uncertainty of 0.02 mm. The cross-sectional area is calculated using A = pi d² / 4. What is the percentage uncertainty in the area? A 1.9%, B 3.8%, C 7.7%, D 15%
steps: Percentage uncertainty in d = 0.02 / 0.52 x 100 = 3.85%.
A is proportional to d², so the percentage uncertainty in A is twice that in d: 2 x 3.85 = 7.7%, option C.
B forgets the power of 2, A halves the percentage, and D squares the percentage itself.

items.question: A student times 20 oscillations of a simple pendulum with a hand-held stopwatch. The main source of uncertainty is the reaction time of the student. Which change would reduce the percentage uncertainty in the period most? A using a stopwatch that reads to 0.001 s, B using a pendulum bob of larger mass, C starting and stopping the stopwatch with the bob at the end of its swing, D timing 40 oscillations and dividing the time by 40
items.answer: D: timing 40 oscillations and dividing the time by 40
steps: The uncertainty from reaction time is about the same fixed amount (for example 0.2 s) however long the timed interval is.
Timing 40 oscillations makes the total time twice as long, so the percentage uncertainty in the time (and in the period) is halved: option D.

A improves the resolution, which is not the limiting factor; B has no effect on the period; C is worse, because the bob is momentarily at rest at the end of its swing and the instant is hard to judge.

items.name: Uncertainties and measurement
items.question: A micrometer screw gauge reads +0.03 mm when its jaws are closed. When used to measure the diameter of a wire it reads 0.78 mm. State the correct diameter of the wire and the type of error present. Explain why taking the mean of several readings does not remove this error.
items.answer: Diameter = 0.75 mm; the error is a systematic (zero) error, which affects every reading by the same amount in the same direction, so averaging does not remove it.
steps: The zero error must be subtracted: 0.78 - 0.03 = 0.75 mm
The error is a systematic (zero) error, not a random error
Every reading is too large by the same amount, so the mean is also too large; averaging only reduces random errors
accept: The correct value can be found by correcting each reading for the zero error
Random errors cause scatter about the true value, which averaging reduces; a systematic error shifts all readings in one direction
The error would be removed by subtracting the zero error or re-zeroing the instrument before use

items.question: The density of a solid metal cylinder is found from its mass, diameter and length. The mass is (62.4 +/- 0.1) g, the diameter is (2.00 +/- 0.02) cm and the length is (7.50 +/- 0.05) cm. Calculate the density of the metal in kg m⁻³, and its absolute uncertainty.
steps: Percentage uncertainties: mass 0.16%; diameter 1.0% (counted twice since V is proportional to d²); length 0.67%.
Total percentage uncertainty = 0.16 + 2 x 1.0 + 0.67 = 2.83%.
Absolute uncertainty = 2.83% of 2648 = 74.9 kg m⁻³, which is about 0.07 × 10³ kg m⁻³, so density = (2.65 +/- 0.07) x 10³ kg m^-3.

items.question: A student determines the acceleration of free fall g with a simple pendulum, using T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g). To measure the period she times 20 oscillations with a stopwatch, starting and stopping it as the bob passes a marker placed at the equilibrium position. Explain why this is better than timing from the end of the swing.
items.answer: The bob is fastest at the equilibrium position, so the crossing instant is well defined; at the end of the swing it is momentarily at rest.
steps: At the equilibrium position the bob has its maximum speed, so the instant it crosses the marker can be judged precisely (the marker gives a clear reference)
At the end of the swing the bob is almost stationary for a short time, so the exact moment is hard to judge and the timing uncertainty is larger
accept: A fiducial marker at the centre gives a fixed reference, reducing judgement and parallax errors
Timing from the same point each time makes the timing more consistent

items.question: The length is measured as (0.800 +/- 0.002) m and the time for 20 oscillations as (35.5 +/- 0.2) s. The value of g from these measurements is 10.02 m s^-2. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in g and state g with its absolute uncertainty.
items.answer: Percentage uncertainty = 1.4%; g = (10.0 +/- 0.1) m s⁻² (absolute uncertainty 0.14 m s⁻²).
steps: Percentage uncertainty in l = 0.002 / 0.800 x 100 = 0.250%.
Percentage uncertainty in the time = 0.2 / 35.5 x 100 = 0.563%, the same as for T.
g = 4 pi² l / T², so the percentage uncertainty in g = 0.250 + 2 x 0.563 = 1.38%.

items.question: The student finds g = 10.02 m s⁻² with an absolute uncertainty of 0.14 m s^-2. The accepted value is 9.81 m s^-2. Deduce whether the student's result is consistent with the accepted value and suggest one possible cause of any discrepancy.
items.answer: Not consistent: 9.81 m s⁻² is outside 9.88 to 10.16 m s⁻²; a systematic error such as l measured to the bottom of the bob.
steps: The range of the result is 10.02 - 0.14 = 9.88 to 10.02 + 0.14 = 10.16 m s⁻²
The accepted value of 9.81 m s⁻² lies outside this range, so the result is not consistent with it (suggesting a systematic error)
A possible cause: l measured to the bottom of the bob instead of its centre, so l is too large and g is too large
accept: Counting one oscillation too many, so the measured period is too small and g is too large
Starting the stopwatch late or stopping it early every time (a systematic timing error), making the period too small
A ruler with a systematic offset (for example a worn end), making l too large

items.question: A capacitor of capacitance C discharges through a resistor of resistance R. The potential difference V across the capacitor at time t is given by V = V0 e^(-t/RC). steps: Take natural logarithms: ln V = ln V0 - t / (RC).

items.name: Graphs and data analysis
items.question: The period T of a pendulum is thought to depend on its length l according to T = k l^n, where k and n are constants. A graph of lg T (y-axis) against lg l (x-axis) is a straight line with gradient 0.50 and y-intercept 0.30. What is the value of k? A 0.30, B 0.50, C 2.0, D 1.35
steps: Take logarithms to base 10: lg T = n lg l + lg k.
The gradient is n = 0.50 and the y-intercept is lg k = 0.30, so k = 10^0.30 = 2.00, which is 2.0 to 2 s.f. (option C).
A gives lg k instead of k, B is the power n, and D uses e^0.30 (natural logarithm) instead of 10^0.30.

items.question: A student plots a graph of T² (y-axis, in s²) against l (x-axis, in m) for a simple pendulum. The best-fit line has a gradient of 4.00 s² m⁻¹ and the worst acceptable line has a gradient of 4.28 s² m^-1. Use T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g) to determine g, and use the percentage uncertainty in the gradient to find the absolute uncertainty in g.
steps: T² = (4 pi² / g) l, so the gradient = 4 pi² / g and g = 4 pi² / gradient.
Uncertainty in the gradient = 4.28 - 4.00 = 0.28 s² m⁻¹, which is 7.0% of 4.00.
The percentage uncertainty in g is the same, so the absolute uncertainty = 7.0% of 9.87 = 0.69 m s⁻²; g = (9.9 +/- 0.7) m s^-2.

items.question: A student adds weights to a spring and measures the extension for each load. The loads are 1.0 N, 2.0 N, 3.0 N, 4.0 N, 5.0 N and 6.0 N and the extensions are 2.1 mm, 4.3 mm, 6.4 mm, 9.9 mm, 10.7 mm and 12.8 mm. items.answer: 9.9 mm at 4.0 N is anomalous (about 8.5 mm expected); repeat that measurement.
steps: The anomalous result is 9.9 mm (at 4.0 N)
The other readings give extension / load of about 2.1 to 2.2 mm per newton, so about 8.5 mm was expected at 4.0 N; 9.9 mm does not fit the pattern
Repeat the measurement at 4.0 N and use the new value instead of the anomalous one (do not include it in the line of best fit)
accept: It may be caused by a misreading, a parallax error or a slip in recording the value
The load may have been disturbed or knocked, or the wrong mass added
Check whether the point is far from the best-fit line on a graph of extension against load
